 Abstract 
 Projected to impact 1.6 million people in the UK by 2040 and cosƟng £25 billion annually, demenƟa 
 presents a growing challenge to society. This study, a pioneering eﬀort to predict the translaƟonal 
 potenƟal of demenƟa research using machine learning, hopes to address the slow translaƟon of 
 fundamental discoveries into pracƟcal applicaƟons despite demenƟa's signiﬁcant societal and economic 
 impact. 
 We used the Dimensions database to extract data from 43,091 UK demenƟa research publicaƟons 
 between the years 1990-2023, speciﬁcally metadata (authors, publicaƟon year etc.), concepts menƟoned 
 in the paper, and the paper abstract. To prepare the data for machine learning we applied methods such 
 as one hot encoding and/or word embeddings. We trained a CatBoost Classiﬁer to predict if a publicaƟon 
 will be cited in a future patent or clinical trial. 
 We trained several model variaƟons. The model combining metadata, concept, and abstract embeddings 
 yielded the highest performance: for patent predicƟons, an Area Under the Receiver OperaƟng 
 CharacterisƟc Curve (AUROC) of 0.84 and 77.17% accuracy; for clinical trial predicƟons, an AUROC of 
 0.81 and 75.11% accuracy. 
 The results demonstrate that integraƟng machine learning within current research methodologies can 
 uncover overlooked publicaƟons, expediƟng the idenƟﬁcaƟon of promising research and potenƟally 
 transforming demenƟa research by predicƟng real-world impact and guiding translaƟonal strategies. 
 1 


 IntroducƟon 
 Almost 1 million people currently live with demenƟa in the UK, [1]  and a recent study forecasts that 1.6 
 million people will be aﬀected in the UK by 2040. [2]  The increasing incidence rate in the 2010s marks a 
 concerning trend reversal compared to other Western naƟons. [3]  , [4]  The economic burden of 
 demenƟa-related diseases, like Alzheimer’s Disease, is substanƟal, cosƟng UK society approximately £25 
 billion annually. [5] 
 At the same Ɵme, the last decade has seen a notable surge in demenƟa research publicaƟons from UK 
 insƟtuƟons, aƩributed to increased government investment since the mid-2010s and the rise of 
 organisaƟons like Alzheimer’s Research UK. [6]  In 2022 alone, over 3,000 demenƟa research papers were 
 published in the UK. [7] 
 This burgeoning research landscape reveals a signiﬁcant gap between scienƟﬁc advancements and 
 tangible health outcomes, [8]  , [9]  underscoring the urgency to expedite and facilitate the translaƟon of 
 fundamental research into real-world beneﬁts for demenƟa paƟents and their families. The vast data 
 processing capabiliƟes of machine learning (ML), analysing extensive data pools within seconds, 
 posiƟons it as a promising potenƟal tool to improve decision-making when addressing this translaƟonal 
 challenge. [10] 
 The slow pace of progress 
 The amyloid hypothesis was postulated more than 30 years ago. [11]  Only in the past 2 years, aŌer 
 hundreds of unsuccessful clinical trials, the ﬁrst two drugs targeƟng beta-amyloid accumulaƟon in the 
 brain demonstrated clinical eﬃcacy in people with early onset Alzheimer’s Disease. [12]  , [13]  This contrasts 
 with the cumulaƟve private expenditure on clinical trials (phases 1-4) for Alzheimer’s Disease, which was 
 esƟmated to be $42.5 billion over a 25-year span. [14]  This esƟmate does not include the cost of the 
 research leading up to those phase 1 trials, which is also notorious for being a lengthy and complicated 
 process: the beginning of the “valley of death” in drug discovery. [15] 
 This is not a problem unique to demenƟa research. In fact, most biomedical research does not translate 
 into meaningful beneﬁts for the people whom the research is trying to serve, [16]  and when it does, it 
 oŌen takes more than two decades to come to fruiƟon. [17] 
 ExplanaƟons about the slow pace of progress in demenƟa research and neuroscience more generally 
 tend to focus on factors such as the complexity of the human brain, [18]  , [19]  the challenges with 
 reproducibility of preclinical data, [20]  or the lower  investment in the ﬁeld of neuroscience compared to 
 other disease areas with similar economic cost to society. [21]  , [22]  While these are all contribuƟng  factors, 
 in this manuscript we build on a concept upstream of all them: it is notoriously diﬃcult to idenƟfy 
 innovaƟve ideas, [23]  , [24] , [25]  and therefore, the  scienƟﬁc community needs new tools to help us decide 
 what pieces of research are more or less likely to lead to translaƟon and paƟent impact. This is where 
 machine learning, with its capacity to handle vast data pools and to locate trends within the data, can 
 play a signiﬁcant role. 
 Peer-review and innovaƟon 
 Peer-review processes, crucial in guiding research funding and publicaƟon decisions, oŌen consider 
 scienƟﬁc quality and potenƟal impact. However, it has been found to be an inconsistent process, [26]  , [27] 
 2 


 and the literature is rich in examples of dispariƟes derived from the peer-review process, related to 
 gender, [28]  , [29]  ethnicity, [30]  research insƟtuƟon, [31]  and geographic locaƟon. [32]  Two recent examples 
 in the ﬁeld of demenƟa research highlighted that the current review model that informs which ideas 
 receive funding and the type of research that is published favours parƟcular researchers over 
 others. [33]  , [34]  This is a considerably well-established  phenomenon, to the point that loƩery systems to 
 award research funding have started being introduced by funding organisaƟons. [35]  , [36] 
 Frameworks to foster translaƟonal impact, such as the Framework to Assess the Impact from 
 TranslaƟonal health research (FAIT), [37]  have been  developed but primarily focus on post-hoc evaluaƟon 
 of research impact. Such frameworks, while valuable, do not inherently expedite the process of 
 translaƟng discoveries into tangible beneﬁts for paƟents. 
 Novel methodologies 
 In recent years, innovaƟve methodologies have emerged to enhance the idenƟﬁcaƟon and evaluaƟon of 
 translaƟonal research. For instance, Manjunath et al. undertook an invenƟve approach by mapping 
 patent citaƟons to research arƟcles. [38]  They revealed  that papers cited by patents possess disƟnct 
 textual, semanƟc, and author demographic characterisƟcs, which can be indicaƟve of their real-world 
 biomedical impact. Similarly, Nelson et al. delved into an extensive analysis of 43.3 million papers, 
 employing deep learning models that amalgamate metadata and abstract text. [39]  Their study 
 concluded that these advanced models are markedly superior to tradiƟonal citaƟon metrics in predicƟng 
 a research paper’s inclusion in patents, guidelines, and policies. ComplemenƟng these ﬁndings, Cao et al. 
 leveraged text mining and predicƟve modelling to explore how the inherent properƟes and network 
 posiƟons of scienƟﬁc concepts facilitate their transiƟon from basic research to pracƟcal applicaƟons. [40] 
 This approach illuminates the intricate pathway of research evoluƟon from theory to pracƟce. 
 More recently, Li et al. introduced a novel TranslaƟonal Progression (TP) measure, rooted in biomedical 
 knowledge representaƟon. [41]  By analysing over 30  million PubMed arƟcles, their method dynamically 
 tracks the trajectory of biomedical research along the translaƟonal conƟnuum, and they argue that their 
 measure could be used by policymakers to monitor biomedical research with high translaƟonal potenƟal 
 in real-Ɵme. 
 CollecƟvely, these methodologies display a signiﬁcant shiŌ in the landscape of research tools and 
 models. They can prove instrumental in bridging the gap between scienƟﬁc discovery and pracƟcal 
 healthcare applicaƟons, a parƟcularly poignant challenge in the ﬁeld of demenƟa research. 
 ContribuƟon to the ﬁeld 
 In this work, we developed an ML model capable of scanning research paper metadata - such as author 
 names, number of authors, research organisaƟons, funders, etc. - and giving a predicƟon on whether 
 that paper will be cited by patents or clinical trials. This tool could, therefore, facilitate the process of 
 idenƟfying fundamental research with the highest “translaƟonal potenƟal”. 
 Alongside paper metadata, we also invesƟgated the impact of content-based features to the models 
 predicƟve analysis. A model that can help understand the translaƟonal potenƟal of research based on 
 the scienƟﬁc content of publicaƟons could have signiﬁcant implicaƟons in the decision-making processes 
 of funders, research organisaƟons or scienƟﬁc journals. 
 3 


 To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst analysis in the demenƟa research ﬁeld, using a novel ML 
 framework, with the potenƟal to predict translaƟon of fundamental research.

 Methods 
 Data availability 
 This paper uses bibliometric available through Dimensions API 
 (hƩps://www.dimensions.ai/products/all-products/dimensions-api/). The code used to extract data from 
 Dimensions, the clean data to create the ML model, and the Python code (version 3.12) created to train 
 the CatBoost ML model are available here: 
 hƩps://github.com/MaƟldaBeinat/ML-for-TranslaƟonal-Research . Any addiƟonal informaƟon can be 
 found upon contact with the authors. 
 Data 
 The dataset was downloaded from Dimensions, a scienƟﬁc database that includes data on 141 million 
 publicaƟons, 158 million patents, 7 million grants and 811 thousand clinical trials (as of January 2024). 
 Dimensions consists of a comprehensive list of publicaƟons linked via citaƟons allowing for a succinct 
 view of the landscape of today’s research, mapping the research cycle from input to output. [7] 
 Metadata on 43,091 publicaƟons in the ﬁeld of demenƟa research was extracted with python code, 
 using Google Colab as our IDE. These publicaƟons were produced by insƟtuƟons based in the United 
 Kingdom between 1990 and 2023. 
 The full feature list can be found in Table S1 along with their deﬁniƟon in Table S2. The feature list 
 comprised of:

 research and disease categorisaƟon,

 - 
 ﬁrst author name, 
 -

 -

 -

 organisaƟon names, 
 -

 - 
 and abstracts. 
 Time sensiƟve metrics provided by Dimensions such as ‘recent citaƟons’, ‘altmetric score’, and ‘Ɵmes 
 cited’ were not included as features in the model due to suspicion of label leakage. Dimensions-provided 
 concepts were included based on their importance score to prevent irrelevant concepts from cluƩering 
 the ML model. To further make sure that less signiﬁcant concepts were not included in the feature list we 
 omiƩed concepts that appeared fewer than twenty Ɵmes in the dataset. Abstract embeddings of 
 individual publicaƟons were included in the feature list  [42] . Titles were excluded to avoid duplicaƟon,  as 
 we found that Ɵtle words were oŌen repeated in the abstract text. We uƟlised OpenAI’s text embedding 
 ADA-02 tool to process abstracts. Long abstracts had to be truncated to meet the tool limitaƟons. We 
 employed a parallel processing technique for the ADA-02 API calls, to reduce the Ɵme it takes to embed 
 all abstracts. [43] 
 When all features in Table S1 were included in the training set, the model performed best, seen by the 
 model metrics.

 Patent and clinical trial data for each publicaƟon was accessed and added. This parƟcular data was used 
 to create the label for the ML model. 
 Data, such as concepts, category research acƟvity code (rac), and category research, condiƟon, and 
 disease categorizaƟon (rcdc), were formaƩed as lists and were one hot encoded. Concepts, category 
 rcdc, category rac, and abstracts required feature reducƟon in the form of Truncated Singular Value 
 DecomposiƟon (TSVD). Data was extracted and analysed from the database with Dimensions Search 
 Language (DSL, an SQL inspired language) and Python 3.12. Using Python on Google Colaboratory, we 
 organised and selected the data for the ML model. GPT4 - via the interface of chatGPT - was used as an 
 aid to the coding process to opƟmise, refactor or improve code. [44] 
 Machine Learning model 
 We selected CatBoostClassiﬁer, among the many ML tools available, [45]  a modern and popular ML 
 classiﬁer used for its high accuracy and ability to handle numerical and categorical data 
 simultaneously. [46]  We used Google Colab as our Python  IDE to clean and prepare data, train the model, 
 and review the results. We used Google colab forms for a user-friendly interface, allowing for a simple 
 way to adjust and alter parameters. We used a variety of libraries to support the analysis, from data 
 processing to training and visualisaƟon. 
 The label was created based on whether the publicaƟon was cited in a patent or clinical trial, allowing 
 the model to predict a publicaƟons inclusion/exclusion from patent/trial. With a classiﬁcaƟon model the 
 label required to be binary: 0 or 1. We chose to label a publicaƟon with ‘0’ if no prior citaƟons within a 
 patent or clinical trial were found in the database, and ‘1’ for publicaƟons with a minimum of 1 citaƟon 
 in a patent or clinical trial. For the purposes of this work, no diﬀerence was made in the classiﬁcaƟon 
 between papers with a single patent citaƟon and papers with mulƟple patent citaƟons. 
 We split the data between 75:25 for training and tesƟng respecƟvely. We opƟmised the model for 
 accuracy, however, the user can choose the performance metric for the model, selecƟng from Accuracy, 
 Precision, Recall, or F1 Score. Furthermore, the user has the opƟon to select the speciﬁc label for training 
 the model, either 'Patents' (label_patents) or 'Clinical Trials' (label_trials)" 
 We rebalanced our dataset due to a disproporƟonate number of publicaƟons without a citaƟon in 
 patents or clinical trials. The majority of the negaƟve class was randomly down sampled by 85% or 95% 
 for patents and clinical trials respecƟvely. Rebalancing of a majority class label is useful to prevent the 
 model from learning only from the majority class, and thus failing to generalise. Oversampling of the 
 minority class of the dataset was not recommended for our dataset as it has been seen to perform 
 poorly when dealing with large datasets, such as ours. [47]  Rebalancing via downsampling led to 1:1.04 
 balance of 1s and 0s (2647 Ones and 2733 Zeros) in the label for patents and 1:1.54 for clinical trials (660 
 Ones and 1011 Zeros) ( Figure S1 ). The rebalanced data set was held throughout training and tesƟng of 
 the model. 
 Models per label 
 For each label, label patents and label clinical trials, three models were trained to examine the eﬀect of 
 diﬀerent feature sets. Model 1, the simplest one for each of the two labels, was trained using 
 publicaƟons’ metadata only. This model provides a baseline to test the model's performance when 
 including content-based informaƟon in the feature set. For both predicƟon problems, Model 2 was 
 trained using metadata alongside concept embeddings. Finally, Model 3 was trained with metadata, 
 concept and abstract embeddings. The ﬁnal model consists of the most elaborate themaƟc data, 
 allowing for the model to learn which characterisƟcs of a publicaƟon, including its scienƟﬁc content 
 extracted from embeddings, led to patent or clinical trial inclusion or exclusion. 
 6 


 The performance for each model was measured by the accuracy, liŌ score, AUC and precision-recall 
 curves. We deﬁned the liŌ score as the accuracy of the model minus the prevalence of zeros in the label 
 input, a way to measure the eﬀecƟveness of the predicƟve model. AUC scores were visualised in an ROC 
 curve, which measures the classiﬁers ability to disƟnguish between the labels. We also used 
 p recision-recall curves, which are more resistant to the bias of an imbalanced datasets. 
 We further analysed the models capability to predict accurately throughout Ɵme by inferring the label of 
 10 randomly selected publicaƟons for each year within our dataset, with equally split posiƟve and 
 negaƟve labels. We ploƩed the ∆ label (real label - predicted label) for each publicaƟon with a threshold 
 of 0.5 and -0.5 to visualise which publicaƟon was labelled inaccurately by the model.

 Results 
 DistribuƟon of publicaƟons 
 Over the period of January 1990 to October 2023, 43,091 demenƟa research papers were published in 
 the United Kingdom. Of these research papers, 3,026 research papers were cited in a patent and 850 
 research papers were cited in a clinical trial. This Ɵmeframe was selected in order to obtain a suﬃciently 
 large number of publicaƟons for analysis, and to allow enough Ɵme for citaƟons from patents and 
 clinical trials to develop. Of these publicaƟons, 36,850 were suitable for analysis, the rest had insuﬃcient 
 data in the features list and were excluded. Taking into account papers published up unƟl 2017, 20,864 
 papers were used to train and test the model. This selecƟon was made during the data preparaƟon 
 phase ( Fig. S1 ). 
 Upon exploring our data set, we found that research papers that were cited in a patent were on average 
 cited by 245.93 other papers, while research papers that were not cited in a patent were on average 
 cited by 30.85 other papers. A two-sample unequal variance t-test conﬁrmed the signiﬁcant diﬀerence 
 on citaƟons (p<0.001). 
 Alongside that, research papers that were cited in clinical trials were on average cited by 382.24 other 
 papers, while papers that were not cited in clinical trials were on average cited by 39.19 other papers. A 
 two-sample unequal variance t-test conﬁrmed the signiﬁcant diﬀerence on citaƟons (p<0.001). 
 The average Ɵme delay from paper publicaƟon to patent citaƟon was 4.28 years ( Fig. S2 ). The average 
 Ɵme delay from publicaƟon to clinical trial citaƟon was 6.57 years ( Fig. S3 ), showing that it takes longer 
 for fundamental research to inﬂuence clinical trials than patents. For the training and tesƟng of our 
 model, we chose to exclude papers published aŌer the year 2017, to allow enough Ɵme for the papers to 
 have been cited in a patent or clinical trial.

 In contrast, the combinaƟon of metadata and concept embeddings as feature input (Model 2) returned

 which was trained just with metadata as feature input. For a full visualisaƟon of the model metrics refer

 Finally, the most complex model for patent predicƟon was trained on metadata, concept embeddings

 We ploƩed the three models’ AUCs onto one Receiver OperaƟng CharacterisƟc (ROC) curve for a beƩer

 ApplicaƟon to other ﬁelds 
 In order to test the models applicability to other ﬁelds, we used the same methodology applied to 
 cancer research papers. We experimented on the predicƟon label for patent inclusion with publicaƟons 
 for breast cancer published between the years 2010 and 2015. We included standard metadata, 
 concepts and abstract embeddings as feature input, downsampling the majority label by 85%. The model 
 resulted with an AUC of 0.81, accuracy of 75.27%, precision of 71.54%, recall of 89.44%, F1 of 75.73%, 
 and liŌ score of 23.24%. The confusion matrix and full metric outputs are in  Table S3 , alongside the ROC 
 curve and precision-recall curve for the breast cancer model in  Fig. S4 .

 Predicted label patents 
 The data we are analysing is highly Ɵme sensiƟve. This stems from the inherent nature of publicaƟons, 
 which require Ɵme to be noƟced, cited, and to contribute value to the ﬁeld – a process beyond our 
 control. Consequently, the label might be aﬀected by Ɵme-dependent factors, for which we do not have 
 explicit controls in the models, yet we raƟﬁed the problem as best we could by removing highly Ɵme 
 dependent features (e.g. recent citaƟons, Ɵmes cited, altmetric scores). To understand the Ɵme 
 sensiƟvity of our models we tested whether the model is capable of predicƟng the label consistently 
 through Ɵme using our test data set. We explored this by randomly selecƟng 5 publicaƟons with label 0 
 and 5 with label 1 for every year within our Ɵmeframe 1990 - 2017, analysing 270 publicaƟons in total. 
 This was done to see the performance of the model through three diﬀerent decades. We compared the 
 real label of each publicaƟon with the predicted label calculated with model 3 for label patents 
 (metadata, concepts and abstract embeddings included as features for predicƟon). The predicted label in 
 this case is the percent chance the model expects the publicaƟon to be cited in a patent: below 50% the 
 model will assign a label 0, above 50% the model assigns a label 1. 
 To determine the diﬀerence between the predicted label and the real label, we ploƩed the ∆ label for

 Discussion 
 This study represents, to our knowledge, the ﬁrst study to predict the translaƟonal potenƟal of demenƟa 
 research using machine learning. By leveraging a comprehensive dataset from Dimensions, 
 encompassing 43,091 publicaƟons, and related data on patents, and clinical trial citaƟons, our ML model 
 provides a novel approach to help highlight research papers that will lead to a patent or clinical trial 
 inclusion. This work addresses a criƟcal need in the ﬁeld of demenƟa research, where the translaƟon of 
 fundamental research into pracƟcal applicaƟons has been notably slow, despite the substanƟal societal 
 and economic burden of the disease. The integraƟon of ML in this context demonstrates a promising 
 avenue for addressing the translaƟonal gap, which research funders and organisaƟons have not been 
 able to successfully close. 
 It is within this context that we see the most promise for models like this one: as a tool that can help aid 
 in the decision-making process. Within our data pool of 43,091 publicaƟons, only 3,026 publicaƟons - or 
 8.99% of the data pool - were cited in a patent or clinical trial. In this work, we present a model that can 
 accurately predict whether a paper will be cited by a patent 77.17% of the Ɵme and can idenƟfy 80.72% 
 of the papers that will go on to be cited by patents. We believe funders, research organisaƟons and even 
 scienƟﬁc publishers could beneﬁt from incorporaƟng tools like this one into their decision-making 
 processes. 
 Model interpretaƟon 
 The classiﬁcaƟon models we created can be used in conjuncƟon with current translaƟonal research 
 methods, such as the FAIT method. [37]  By integraƟng  our ML model with these methods, we can 
 uncover overlooked publicaƟons and expedite the idenƟﬁcaƟon of promising research. This synergy is 
 crucial for advancing the ﬁeld of demenƟa research, where the slow pace of progress and high failure 
 rates in clinical trials have been long standing challenges. 
 ClassiﬁcaƟon models are most useful to categorise parƟcular datasets into predeﬁned classes. Such 
 models have one of two outputs: probabilisƟc or categorical. Our model outputs two possible categories: 
 1 or 0. The applicaƟon of ML in this context is parƟcularly promising, as it enables the handling of vast 
 and complex datasets, a task impracƟcal for tradiƟonal methods, simply by categorisaƟon. Our approach, 
 which combines various data features, demonstrates the capacity of ML models to unravel intricate 
 paƩerns and associaƟons within academic research that has the capability to predict real-world impact. 
 Working with large data sets, such as this, it is crucial to work with models that are eﬀecƟve and can 
 achieve high accuracy levels, such as classiﬁcaƟon models. Further, classiﬁcaƟon models can handle very 
 unbalanced datasets, and with the nature of our dataset, it is more likely to encounter unbalanced 
 datasets, with preference towards negaƟve labels. Most importantly, they are very suitable for real-Ɵme 
 predicƟons, essenƟal in the ﬁeld of translaƟonal research where predicƟng a paper's potenƟal for 
 further applicaƟons can speed up the process from basic research to clinical pracƟce. 
 In developing our model, we drew inspiraƟon from pioneering works in the ﬁeld: Manjunath et al 
 correlate patent citaƟons with research arƟcles which revealed disƟnct textual, semanƟc, and author 
 demographic characterisƟcs that could predict real-world impact. [38]  This methodology informed our 
 decision to use patent citaƟons as a measure of a paper's translaƟonal potenƟal. Nelson et al on the 
 other hand uƟlised deep learning models to analyse extensive databases, they demonstrated the 
 superiority of advanced ML models over tradiƟonal citaƟon metrics in predicƟng a research paper’s 
 inclusion in patents and policies. [39]  We incorporated  similar techniques, emphasising the role of 
 16 


 abstract embeddings in predicƟng research impact. Cao et al further leveraged text mining and 
 predicƟve modelling, exploring the transiƟon of scienƟﬁc concepts from basic research to pracƟcal 
 applicaƟons. [40]  Their approach inﬂuenced our analysis  of the content and context of research papers, 
 speciﬁcally the inclusion of concepts and themes idenƟﬁed in publicaƟons. Finally, Li et al. introduced a 
 novel TranslaƟonal Progression (TP) measure, tracking the trajectory of biomedical research along the 
 translaƟonal conƟnuum. [41]  Our methodology was inspired  by their dynamic approach, using 
 biomedical knowledge representaƟon to idenƟfy high-potenƟal research. 
 Our approach demonstrates the capacity of ML to analyse complex data sets. The inclusion of concept 
 and abstract embeddings substanƟally improves the ML model's predicƟve accuracy, indicaƟng the 
 importance of themaƟc and lexical analysis in classifying publicaƟons. Importantly, our model can predict 
 the potenƟal of newly published papers for inclusion in patents or clinical trials, demonstraƟng its 
 applicability in real-Ɵme assessment of research impact. 
 Model performance 
 We show that through analysis of standard metadata points, such as the number of authors in a 
 publicaƟon, predicƟon outputs are inferior to those aƩained via high dimensional vectors. Our analysis 
 shows that the inclusion of concept and abstract embeddings, depicƟng overarching themes and trends 
 within the publicaƟon, substanƟally improves the ML models predicƟon accuracy. The inclusion of 
 concept and abstract embeddings shows us that the ML model extracts important informaƟon about 
 themes necessary to classify publicaƟons. 
 Importantly, the ML model is capable of predicƟng whether newly published papers have potenƟal for 
 inclusion in patent or clinical trials. This signiﬁes that through the correct frameworks it is feasible to 
 execute high ﬁdelity outputs that provide the ﬁeld with a succinct path for translaƟonal output. 
 Contrary to tradiƟonal approaches that heavily rely on citaƟon metrics, our ﬁndings suggest that these 
 are not the sole indicators of a publicaƟon's impact. Our ML model eﬀecƟvely idenƟﬁes research likely to 
 lead to patent or clinical trial citaƟons without depending on Ɵme-sensiƟve data such as altmetric scores 
 or the number of citaƟons. This ﬁnding is pivotal in redeﬁning the metrics used for assessing the 
 translaƟonal potenƟal of research. 
 We now have the opƟon to incorporate machine learning models, with the capability to analyse complex 
 themaƟc based data, with our quanƟtaƟve metrics, enabling us to idenƟfy themes and trajectories with 
 the highest translaƟonal potenƟal. We can use a supervised learning method, such as a classiﬁcaƟon 
 model, alongside unsupervised dimensionality reducƟon methods that capture large texts, translaƟng 
 from a high dimensional vector to a low dimensional space, to enrich our data analyses. Research 
 suggests that using an enƟre body of text, rather than concepts and abstract embeddings only, may 
 result in higher ﬁdelity. [39]  On the other hand,  there has been opposing research staƟng that while 
 embeddings may be eﬀecƟve in shorter texts, model performance has been seen to increase with 
 abstract embeddings, challenging the noƟon that whole text embeddings may be superior. [48]  However, 
 the exploraƟon of whole text embeddings versus abstract embedding only was outside the scope of our 
 research. 
 LimitaƟons 
 While our study marks signiﬁcant progress, it is not without limitaƟons. The largest challenge lies with 
 the nature of the publicaƟons, parƟcularly their requirement of Ɵme for patent or clinical trial inclusions. 
 We aƩempted to recƟfy this limitaƟon by removing Ɵme sensiƟve features that could leak the label to 
 17 


 the model. This in turn allows for the applicaƟon of the model to newly published papers and removes 
 Ɵme as an obstacle in the models predicƟon. 
 The secondary challenge lies in the reliance on citaƟons in patents and clinical trials as proxies for 
 translaƟonal impact. This approach, while pracƟcal, may not fully capture the mulƟfaceted nature of 
 research impact. However, based on research by Manjunath et al., papers cited by patents seem to have 
 disƟnct characterisƟcs that are indicaƟve of real-world impact. Based on the models increasing 
 performance when including themaƟc based features, we believe our model is extracƟng intricate 
 characterisƟcs for patent and clinical trial predicƟon. [38]  We believe that due to the models increased 
 predicƟve analysis, with features such as concept and abstract embeddings, provides a deeper 
 understanding of otherwise impossible to understand informaƟon. [39]  Even so, patent-cited arƟcles are 
 idenƟﬁed as a unique subset of biomedical literature, characterised by diﬀerences in scienƟﬁc domain, 
 research team composiƟon, and language use. This uniqueness poses a challenge in generalising ﬁndings 
 across diﬀerent subsets of literature. This constraint however is amended by the models applicability to 
 mulƟple diﬀerent domains, seen by its applicaƟon to breast cancer research by our model alongside 
 research presented by Cao et al. and Li et al. [40] ,  [41] 
 The complexity of the classiﬁcaƟon model, or any ML model, is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it is 
 capable of idenƟfying and learning from complex paƩerns in data samples. On the other hand, this very 
 complexity makes it challenging to pinpoint which features of the model are most inﬂuenƟal in 
 determining its performance. EssenƟally, it's diﬃcult to simplify the model to just its most impacƞul 
 elements due to its intricate nature. This implicaƟon prevents the understanding of the model. However, 
 this limitaƟon is not the real problem to translaƟonal research, in reality it is crucial and the most 
 beneﬁcial method. It is important to understand the diﬀerence between simplicity of the method and 
 explainability. While current frameworks for translaƟonal research are explainable and easily understood 
 by the wider public, it is clear that their funcƟon is not eﬀecƟve. ML models, whether supervised or 
 unsupervised, can be complex to explain. Although it's oŌen diﬃcult to isolate individual features to 
 understand their speciﬁc contribuƟons, these models funcƟon in a straighƞorward and eﬀecƟve way. 
 They provide a more accurate representaƟon of the complex research they are used to analyse. [43]  The 
 simplicity of models can be disadvantageous as they do not adequately represent the complexity of 
 research such as that encountered here. 
 Our model's feature weighƟng is not enƟrely transparent, and it might be subject to biases. [33],  [34],  [35],  [36] 
 Biases may be the result of mulƟple factors, such as unbalanced data for certain classes of papers, or 
 underrepresentaƟon of certain subpopulaƟons in scienƟﬁc literature. While there are several methods 
 to test models against speciﬁc biases, [49]  this test  was beyond the scope of the current research. At the 
 same Ɵme, it should be noted that our model goes beyond simple citaƟon counts used by current 
 methodologies, analysing content and themes, potenƟally oﬀering a more balanced view of a paper's

 Machine learning models that use standard metadata and complex themaƟc analysis (such as concepts

 clinical trial, providing a pathway towards impact. Our work advocates for a shiŌ towards the use of

Abstract: Projected to impact 1.6 million people in the UK by 2040 and cosƟng £25 billion annually, demenƟa presents a growing challenge to society. This study, a pioneering eﬀort to predict the translaƟonal potenƟal of demenƟa research using machine learning, hopes to address the slow translaƟon of fundamental discoveries into pracƟcal applicaƟons despite demenƟa's signiﬁcant societal and economic impact. We used the Dimensions database to extract data from 43,091 UK demenƟa research publicaƟons between the years 1990-2023, speciﬁcally metadata (authors, publicaƟon year etc.), concepts menƟoned in the paper, and the paper abstract.
